name: Curved and Angular Interiors Rating
description: Faithful replication with the original images: 56 rendered interiors from a neuroarchitecture study of curved versus angular form. Seven abstract spatial scenarios (two thresholds A1-A2, two corridors B1-B2, three seating spaces C1-C3) are each rendered in eight versions: background geometry (angular / curved) x foreground figure geometry (angular / curved) x colour (orange figures on a white background / white figures on an orange background). Participants see all 56 images in random order, self-paced, and for each one rate seven qualities on a 1-5 scale (liking, beauty, curvature, angularity, fascination, coherence, hominess), tick the emotions they feel from eight words (interested, excited, uplifted, alert, stressed, irritable, confused, afraid), estimate how many minutes they would comfortably stay there (0-200), judge whether the space is more likely public or private, and click the cell of a 3 x 3 grid over the image where their eyes were drawn (optional). Age and gender are asked at the end. Rebuilt from Wei, Chuquichambi, Damiano, Bruce & Walther (2026), A design-integrated framework for neuroarchitectural research, Frontiers in Psychology 17: 1666480 (Phase 1 image survey), with the images cropped from its Figure 2 (CC BY 4.0). Image ids: scenario_colour_geometry, e.g. A1_W_ac = threshold 1, white background, angular background with a curved foreground figure (first letter background, second foreground, a = angular, c = curved; W = white background, O = orange background). Analysis as in the paper: compare the ratings across background geometry, foreground geometry and colour (within-participant factorial, e.g. mixed models with participant as random effect) and check agreement on the curvature and angularity ratings; the paper reports that the intended curved/angular distinctions were clearly perceived with high agreement between participants, and that foreground geometry influenced several evaluative ratings more than background geometry (foreground-sensitive preferences for curvature). Differences from the original study: (1) the paper names the rated qualities, the 1-5 scale, the 0-200 minute range, the public/private choice and the 3 x 3 grid but does not print the question wording or scale labels, so all question stems and anchors (1 = not at all, 5 = very much) are ours; (2) the emotion list is adapted from PANAS in the paper but not printed; the eight words are the ones found in the authors' shared data (OSF), their order is ours; (3) the age and gender questions are ours; (4) the images are the figure copies (about 300 px), not the full-size renders; (5) the paper's later phases (3D-printed prototype, full-scale installation, VR and biosensors) are not included.
author: Wei, Chuquichambi, Damiano, Bruce & Walther
